claim: Cell mechanical properties determine many physiological functions, such as cell fate specification, migration, or circulation through vasculature.
source: Cell mechanical properties determine many physiological functions, such as cell fate specification, migration, or circulation through vasculature.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell mechanics presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but draws on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The study combines mechanical characterization of cells across a variety of mouse and human systems with machine learning-based discriminative network analysis of associated transcriptomic profiles.
source: We combine mechanical characterization of cells across a variety of mouse and human systems with machine learning-based discriminative network analysis of associated transcriptomic profiles to infer a conserved network module of five genes with putative roles in cell mechanics regulation.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: The study identified a conserved network module of five genes with putative roles in cell mechanics regulation.
source: We combine mechanical characterization of cells across a variety of mouse and human systems with machine learning-based discriminative network analysis of associated transcriptomic profiles to infer a conserved network module of five genes with putative roles in cell mechanics regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by the network analysis results.

claim: The identified gene markers are universal, trustworthy, and specific to the mechanical phenotype across the studied mouse and human systems.
source: We validate in silico that the identified gene markers are universal, trustworthy, and specific to the mechanical phenotype across the studied mouse and human systems
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico validation results presented in the study.

claim: CAV1 changes the mechanical phenotype of cells when silenced or overexpressed.
source: demonstrate experimentally that a selected target, CAV1, changes the mechanical phenotype of cells accordingly when silenced or overexpressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental perturbation data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Cell stiffness is a sensitive label-free biophysical marker of cell state in health and disease.
source: Since the mechanical phenotype of cells has been shown to reflect functional cell changes, it is now well established as a sensitive label-free biophysical marker of cell state in health and disease (Guck and Chilvers, 2013; Nematbakhsh and Lim, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell stiffness is involved in processes such as development and cancer progression.
source: Beyond being a passive property that can be correlated with cell state, cell stiffness is increasingly recognized as an important feature involved in processes such as development (Lecuit and Lenne, 2007; Hannezo and Heisenberg, 2019) and cancer progression (Suresh, 2007; Gensbittel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The actin cortex and its contractility regulated via Rho signaling is the most prominent contributor to the global mechanical phenotype.
source: According to current knowledge, the most prominent contributor to the global mechanical phenotype is the actin cortex and its contractility regulated via Rho signaling (Chugh and Paluch, 2018; Kelkar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field as indicated by the citations.

claim: Intermediate filaments, including vimentin and keratin, can contribute to measured cell stiffness, especially at high strains.
source: Intermediate filaments, including vimentin and keratin, reside deeper inside the cell and can also contribute to measured cell stiffness, especially at high strains (Seltmann et al., 2013; Patteson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microtubules contribute to cell stiffness at high strains.
source: Although there is some evidence of the contribution of microtubules to cell stiffness at high strains (Kubitschke et al., 2017), their role has been difficult to address directly, since drug-induced microtubule disassembly evokes reinforcement of actin cytoskeleton and cell contractility (Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cell mechanical phenotype can be influenced by the level of intracellular packing.
source: Apart from cytoskeletal contributions, the cell mechanical phenotype can be influenced by the level of intracellular packing (Zhou et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cell mechanical phenotype can be influenced by mechanical properties of organelles occupying the cell interior, such as the cell nucleus.
source: Apart from cytoskeletal contributions, the cell mechanical phenotype can be influenced by the level of intracellular packing (Zhou et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2017) or mechanical properties of organelles occupying the cell interior, such as the cell nucleus (Caille et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RT-DC is a microfluidics-based method that enables rapid analysis of thousands of cells.
source: The mechanical phenotypes of the different cell states within each dataset were characterized primarily using real-time deformability cytometry (RT-DC), a microfluidics-based method that enables rapid analysis of thousands of cells (Otto et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a description of the RT-DC method supported by citation and reference to a figure.

claim: RT-DC relies on flowing cells through a narrow constriction of a microfluidic channel and high-speed imaging to assess cell deformation.
source: RT-DC relies on flowing cells through a narrow constriction of a microfluidic channel and high-speed imaging to assess the ensuing cell deformation (Otto et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This describes the RT-DC methodology with citation and figure references.

claim: In RT-DC, the mechanical phenotype is quantified by an apparent Young's modulus deduced from cell size and deformation.
source: In the context of this method, the mechanical phenotype is understood as whole-cell elasticity quantified by an apparent Young's modulus, E, deduced from cell size and deformation under given experimental conditions (Mokbel et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This describes how mechanical phenotype is quantified in RT-DC, supported by citation and figure reference.

claim: Higher Young's modulus values indicate that a cell is more difficult to deform, or stiffer.
source: Young's modulus quantifies how much stress (force per unit area) is necessary to deform a cell to a certain extent (i.e., strain), thus higher Young's modulus values indicate that a cell is more difficult to deform, or stiffer.
evidence: This is a definition based on established physical principles.

claim: The study curated mechano-transcriptomic data assemblies originating from five different biological systems.
source: We curated mechano-transcriptomic data assemblies originating from five different biological systems (Figure 2) that included a total of eight transcriptomic datasets (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the data curation process with references to figures and tables.

claim: Two transcriptomic datasets were used for target prediction, and six for target validation.
source: Two of the transcriptomic datasets were used for target prediction, and the reaming six for target validation.
evidence: This describes the allocation of datasets in the study methodology.

claim: Glioblastoma cells with higher STAT3-Ser/Hes3 activation have a stiffer phenotype.
source: As previously demonstrated, the higher the STAT3-Ser/Hes3 activation in the characterized states, the stiffer the measured phenotype of glioblastoma cells (Poser et al., 2019; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Small-cell carcinoma cells have a lower apparent Young's modulus compared to adenocarcinoma cells across intestine, lung, and stomach tissues.
source: Consistently across tissues, small cell-carcinoma cells had a lower apparent Young's modulus compared to their adenocarcinoma counterparts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Small-cell carcinomas have comparatively small cell sizes, short doubling times and high metastatic potential, all connected with poor clinical prognosis in patients.
source: Small-cell carcinomas have comparatively small cell sizes, short doubling times and high metastatic potential, all connected with poor clinical prognosis in patients (Brenner et al., 2004; Kalemkerian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical literature.

claim: MCF10A cells bearing single-allele oncogenic mutation H1047R in PIK3CA show increased stiffness compared to wild-type control.
source: In the third studied system, a non-tumorigenic breast epithelium MCF10A cell line bearing single-allele oncogenic mutation H1047R in the catalytic subunit alpha of the phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase (PIK3CA) (Juvin et al., 2013; Kiselev et al., 2015) showed increased stiffness compared to the wild-type (WT) control (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data in Figure 2C and citations to previous work on the cell line.

claim: H1047R mutation causes constitutive activation of PIK3CA and aberrant triggering of the PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling pathway leading to growth factor-independent proliferation.
source: H1047R mutation causes constitutive activation of PIK3CA and an aberrant triggering of the PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling pathway leading to growth factor-independent proliferation (Bader et al., 2006; Kang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the mutation.

claim: Fuzzy-colony forming (F-class) iPSCs have lower stiffness compared to compact-colony forming (C-class) iPSCs.
source: In the fourth system, the fuzzy-colony forming (F-class) state of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) had a lower stiffness as compared to the bone-fide compact-colony forming (C-class) state (Urbanska et al., 2017; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C-class iPSCs establish endogenous expression of reprogramming factors at moderate levels, while F-class iPSCs depend on ectopic expression and are characterized by fast proliferation.
source: C-class cells establish endogenous expression of reprogramming factors at moderate levels toward the end of reprogramming, while F-class cells depend on the ectopic expression of the pluripotency factors and are characterized by a fast proliferation rate (Tonge et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Newborn neurons have higher apparent Young's moduli than proliferating progenitors.
source: Finally, we characterized two stages of developing neurons isolated from embryonic mouse brain (Aprea et al., 2013), and observed that the newborn neurons (NNs) had higher apparent Young's moduli than proliferating progenitors (PPs) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2E and citation to the source of the cells.

claim: PC-corr combines loadings from principal component analysis and Pearson's correlation for every pair of genes.
source: To this end, we utilized a method for inferring phenotype-associated functional network modules from omics datasets termed PC-corr (Ciucci et al., 2017), that relies on combining loadings obtained from the principal component (PC) analysis and Pearson's correlation for every pair of genes.
evidence: This describes the PC-corr methodology with citation to the original method.

claim: PC-corr incorporates the relative relevance of each feature for discriminating between conditions, not just gene co-expression.
source: Owing to the combination of the Pearson's correlation coefficient and the discriminative information included in the PC loadings, the PC-corr analysis does not only consider gene co-expression — as is the case for classical co-expression network analysis — but also incorporates the relative relevance of each feature for discriminating between two or more conditions; in our case, the conditions representing soft and stiff phenotypes.
evidence: This explains the advantage of PC-corr over classical co-expression analysis based on the method's design.

claim: The conserved functional network module comprises five genes: CAV1, FHL2, IGFBP7, TAGLN, and THBS1.
source: We focused on the five genes from this conserved network module as putative targets for regulating cell mechanics: CAV1, FHL2, IGFBP7, TAGLN, and THBS1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study identifying the five target genes.

claim: CAV1 is a structural component of caveolae involved in mechanoprotective mechanism of buffering plasma membrane tension.
source: Caveolin-1, CAV1, is a protein most prominently known for its role as a structural component of caveolae. Caveolae are small cup-shaped invaginations in the cell membrane that are involved, among other functions, in the mechanoprotective mechanism of buffering the plasma membrane tension (Sinha et al., 2011; Parton and del Pozo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on CAV1 function.

claim: CAV1 can confer its mechanoprotective role independently of caveolae.
source: Recent data suggests that CAV1 can also confer its mechanoprotective role independently of caveolae (Lolo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: CAV1 plays a role in metabolic regulation and Rho-signaling.
source: Apart from membrane organization and membrane domain scaffolding, CAV1 plays a role in an array of regulatory functions such as metabolic regulation or Rho-signaling (Parton and del Pozo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: FHL2 is a multifaceted LIM domain protein with many binding partners and transcription factor activity.
source: The second identified target, four and a half LIM domains 2, FHL2, is a multifaceted LIM domain protein with many binding partners and a transcription factor activity (Johannessen et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on FHL2.

claim: FHL2 remains bound to actin filaments under high tension and is shuttled to the nucleus under low cytoskeletal tension.
source: FHL2 has recently been shown to remain bound to actin filaments under high tension, and be shuttled to the nucleus under low cytoskeletal tension (Nakazawa et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research on FHL2 function.

claim: IGFBP7 is a secreted protein implicated in a variety of cancers and involved in regulation of cell proliferation, adhesion, and senescence.
source: The third target, Insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 7, IGFBP7, is a secreted protein implicated in a variety of cancers. It is involved in the regulation of processes such as cell proliferation, adhesion, and senescence (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on IGFBP7.

claim: Transgelin is an actin-binding protein whose expression is upregulated by high cytoskeletal tension.
source: Transgelin, TGLN, is an actin-binding protein whose expression is upregulated by high cytoskeletal tension (Liu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Transgelin plays a role in cancer.
source: Transgelin, TGLN, is an actin-binding protein whose expression is upregulated by high cytoskeletal tension (Liu et al., 2017) and is also known to play a role in cancer (Dvorakova et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: THBS1 is a matricellular, calcium-binding glycoprotein that mediates cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesions and has many regulatory functions.
source: Finally, thrombospondin 1, THBS1, is a matricellular, calcium-binding glycoprotein that mediates cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesions and has many regulatory functions (Adams and Lawler, 2011; Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on THBS1.

claim: The target genes show clear differences in expression levels between soft and stiff cell states and provide for clustering of samples corresponding to different cell stiffnesses.
source: The target genes show clear differences in expression levels between the soft and stiff cell states and provide for clustering of the samples corresponding to different cell stiffnesses in both prediction and validation datasets (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The direction of expression changes between soft and stiff cell states in validation datasets was not always following the same direction.
source: The direction of changes in the expression levels between the soft and stiff cell states in the validation datasets was not always following the same direction (Figure 4C–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Genes associated with cell mechanics may not have a monotonic relationship with cell stiffness, but rather are characterized by different expression regimes.
source: This suggests that the genes associated with cell mechanics may not have a monotonic relationship with cell stiffness, but rather are characterized by different expression regimes in which the expression change in opposite directions can have the same effect on cell stiffness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed non-monotonic expression patterns.

claim: The importance of specific targets for mechanical phenotype change may vary depending on the origin of the sample.
source: This indicates that the importance of specific targets for the mechanical phenotype change may vary depending on the origin of the sample.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations of variable expression changes across different samples.

claim: The combinatorial marker had a minimum AUC-ROC of 0.97 for positive hypothesis I (universality across systems).
source: the combinatorial marker outperformed the individual genes with a minimum AUC-ROC of 0.97.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: CAV1, FHL2, and TAGLN showed particularly high minimum AUC-ROC values (≥0.78) for positive hypothesis I.
source: Particularly high minimum AUC-ROC values (≥0.78) were obtained for CAV1, FHL2, and TAGLN
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The combinatorial marker had an AUC-ROC value of 0.92 for positive hypothesis II (universality across data sources).
source: The combinatorial marker had an AUC-ROC value of 0.92.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: For the negative hypothesis (tissue specificity), the combinatorial marker had a min AUC-ROC value equivalent to a random classifier (0.51).
source: For the combinatorial marker, the min AUC-ROC value was equivalent to a random classifier (0.51)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The discriminative power of the obtained markers vanished when tested on groups that do not encompass cell mechanic phenotype difference, indicating the markers are specific to the mechanical phenotype.
source: Since the discriminative power of the obtained markers vanished (reached AUC-ROC close to 0.50 corresponding to a random classifier) when tested on groups that do not encompass cell mechanic phenotype difference, we can conclude that the identified markers are specific to the mechanical phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative hypothesis testing results.

claim: The combinatorial marker had remarkably low JVT p values (p = 0.01) in positive hypotheses I and II.
source: As summarized in Table 4, the combinatorial marker had remarkably low JVT p values (p = 0.01) in positive hypotheses I and II
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the trustworthiness analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: In the negative hypothesis, the JVT p value of the combinatorial marker is not significant (p = 0.91).
source: Conversely, in the negative hypothesis, the JVT p value of the combinatorial marker is not significant (p = 0.91).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the trustworthiness analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: TGBC cells have higher levels of CAV1 compared to ECC4 cells on a protein level.
source: Before perturbations, we confirmed that TGBC cells have higher levels of CAV1 compared to ECC4 cells on a protein level (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TGBC cells are characterized by a stiffer phenotype compared to ECC4 cells when measured with RT-DC, AFM indentation, and AFM microrheology.
source: and that they are characterized by a stiffer phenotype, not only when measured with RT-DC (Figures 2B and 5B), but also with AFM using both standard indentation experiments (Figure 5C), as well as oscillatory measurements at different frequencies, referred to as AFM microrheology (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mechanical characterization data shown in multiple figures.

claim: RT-DC measurements yielded higher apparent Young's moduli compared to AFM indentation for the same cell line.
source: Even though the apparent Young's moduli obtained for TGBCS cells were consistently higher than those for ECC4 cells across all three methods, the absolute values measured for a given cell line varied depending on the methods: RT-DC measurements yielded higher apparent Young's moduli compared to AFM indentation
evidence: This is an observation from comparing measurements across different methods.

claim: Apparent Young's moduli derived from AFM microrheology measurements were frequency-dependent and fell between RT-DC and AFM indentation values.
source: while the apparent Young's moduli derived from AFM microrheology measurements were frequency-dependent and fell between the other two methods (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing measurements across different methods shown in figures.

claim: The observed increase in apparent Young's modulus with probing frequency aligns with previous findings on cell stiffening with increased probing rates.
source: The observed increase in apparent Young's modulus with probing frequency aligns with previous findings on cell stiffening with increased probing rates observed for both AFM indentation (Li et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2012) and microrheology assays (Alcaraz et al., 2003; Massiera et al., 2007; Rigato et al., 2017).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All RNAi approaches for CAV1 knock-down resulted in decreased apparent Young's modulus of TGBC cells as measured by RT-DC.
source: All the RNAi approaches resulted in the decrease of the apparent Young's modulus of TGBC cells as measured by RT-DC (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from the perturbation experiments shown in figures.

claim: CAV1 knock-down with esiCAV1-1 resulted in decreased stiffness of TGBC cells using AFM indentation and microrheology.
source: We further confirmed that CAV1 knock-down with esiCAV1-1 resulted in decreased stiffness of TGBC cells using AFM indentation (Figure 5G) and microrheology (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is a finding from the perturbation experiments shown in figures.

claim: Fluorescence-positive cells in the CAV1-transfected sample showed higher apparent Young's moduli compared to fluorescence-negative cells in both control and CAV1-transfected samples.
source: The fluorescence-positive cells in the CAV1-transfected sample, CAV1iT+, showed higher apparent Young's moduli as compared to fluorescence-negative cells in both control sample (mock) and CAV1-transfected sample (CAV1iT–, internal control) (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This is a finding from the overexpression experiments shown in figures.

claim: The effect of CAV1 overexpression was more pronounced in TGBC cells compared to ECC4 cells.
source: The effect was observed in ECC4 as well as TGBC cells. However, it was more pronounced in the TGBC cells, suggesting that the cells may be more responsive to the artificial increase in CAV1 levels when natively expressing a basal level of this protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the overexpression experiments with an interpretation.

claim: TAM treatment of MCF10A-ER-Src cells triggers Src phosphorylation and cellular transformation.
source: As previously shown, TAM addition triggers Src phosphorylation and cellular transformation (Hirsch et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: TAM-induced MCF10A-ER-Src cells show acquisition of a soft phenotype evident at 36 hr post induction after a transient stiffening.
source: which is associated with F-actin cytoskeletal changes and, after a transient stiffening, the acquisition of a soft phenotype evident at 36 hr post induction (Tavares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The expression of CAV1 diminishes over time after TAM treatment in MCF10A-ER-Src cells.
source: We inspected a previously published microarray dataset and determined that the expression of CAV1 diminishes over time after TAM treatment (Hirsch et al., 2010; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of published data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The decrease of CAV1 could be observed at the protein level 72 hr post TAM induction in MCF10A-ER-Src cells.
source: We then showed that the decrease of CAV1 could be observed at the protein level 72 hr post induction (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TAM-induced MCF10A-ER-Src cells show a significant decrease in cell stiffness at 72 hr post induction.
source: a timepoint at which the TAM-induced MCF10A-ER-Src cells show a significant decrease in cell stiffness (Tavares et al., 2017 and Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knocking down CAV1 decreased the stiffness of uninduced MCF10A-ER-Src cells.
source: We next showed that knocking down CAV1 decreased the stiffness of uninduced MCF10A-ER-Src cells (Figure 6D), similar to the effect of TAM induction.
evidence: This is a finding from the perturbation experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Rescuing CAV1 levels in TAM-induced MCF10A-ER-Src cells by transient overexpression resulted in cells showing a stiff phenotype corresponding to uninduced cells.
source: Finally, we performed an inverse experiment, in which we rescued the CAV1 levels in TAM-induced MCF10A-ER-Src cells by transient overexpression. The cells with CAV1 overexpression showed a stiff phenotype, corresponding to the one of uninduced cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The results show that CAV1 not only correlates with, but also is causative of mechanical phenotype change.
source: Taken together, the results obtained with the intestine carcinoma cell lines and MCF10A-ER-Src cells show that CAV1 not only correlates with, but also is causative of mechanical phenotype change.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the perturbation experiments across multiple cell systems.

claim: The mechanomics approach presented combines omics data with mechanical phenotypes across different systems to identify genes that ubiquitously contribute to cell mechanical phenotype in a hypothesis-free manner.
source: The systematic approach presented here, combining omics data with mechanical phenotypes across different systems, has the power to identify genes that ubiquitously contribute to cell mechanical phenotype in a hypothesis-free manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the approach and its capabilities.

claim: The identified genes can be used as knobs for adjusting mechanical cell properties to explore their role in homeostasis or to therapeutically intervene in relevant pathologies.
source: Such genes can, in the future, be used as knobs for adjusting mechanical cell properties to explore their role in the homeostasis of multicellular systems or to therapeutically intervene in relevant pathologies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the findings.

claim: The workflow presented is a blueprint for data-driven discovery of cell mechanics markers that can serve as targets for modulating cell mechanical properties.
source: The workflow presented here is a blueprint for data-driven discovery of cell mechanics markers that can serves as targets for modulating cell mechanical properties.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Key features of the approach are hypothesis-free modus operandi and integration of information from different biological systems.
source: Its key features are the hypothesis-free modus operandi and the integration of information from different biological systems, that allows to focus on genes that play a relatively general role in cell mechanics rather than on genes specific to the individual experimental models.
evidence: This describes the key methodological features of the approach.

claim: PC-corr offers a multivariate alternative to classical co-expression analysis by highlighting correlation between genes and their relative importance for separating samples based on mechanical phenotype.
source: Noteworthy, by including the PC loadings in the scores used for thresholding, the PC-corr method implemented for network analysis in our study offers a multivariate alternative to classical co-expression analysis, that highlights not only the correlation between the genes but also their relative importance for separating samples based on their mechanical phenotype.
evidence: This explains the advantage of the PC-corr method used in the study.

claim: PC-corr offers robust performance on different types of omics data and has proven efficacy in several studies.
source: Despite its simplicity, PC-corr offers a robust performance on different types of omics data, and has already proven its efficacy in several studies (Ciucci et al., 2017; Poser et al., 2019; Durán et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using PC-corr.

claim: The mechanical phenotype of single cells is a global readout of cell's resistance to deformation that integrates contributions from all cellular components.
source: The mechanical phenotype of single cells is a global readout of cell's resistance to deformation that integrates contributions from all cellular components.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of mechanical phenotype based on established understanding.

claim: At low deformations (<3 µm), the actin cortex is believed to dominate the measured mechanical response.
source: The three techniques implemented for measuring cell mechanics in this study — RT-DC, AFM indentation, and AFM microrheology — exert comparatively low deformations (<3 µm, see Supplementary file 1), at which the actin cortex is believed to dominate the measured response.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cell mechanics at different deformation levels.

claim: Other cellular components including membrane, microtubules, intermediate filaments, nucleus, other organelles, and cytoplasmic packing can contribute to measured deformations.
source: However, other cellular components, including the membrane, microtubules, intermediate filaments, nucleus, other organelles, and cytoplasmic packing, can also contribute to the measured deformations (reviewed in detail in Urbanska and Guck, 2024)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a review article.

claim: The study did not observe enrichment of gene ontology terms related to actin cytoskeleton organization, actomyosin contractility, or cell migration among the target genes.
source: Among the target genes elucidated in our analysis, we did not observe enrichment of gene ontology terms related to actin cytoskeleton organization, actomyosin contractility, or cell migration — processes that are typically associated with cell mechanics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the gene ontology analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The lack of obvious cell mechanics-related GO terms may indicate that the association of the identified genes with cell mechanics is relatively unknown.
source: The fact that these GO terms are not obviously related to cell mechanics might be an indicator that the association of the identified genes with cell mechanics is relative unknown, and that our mechanomics approach can identify such associations de novo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO analysis results.

claim: The upregulated genes in stiff cells are associated with negative regulation of growth and transcription, pointing toward targeted reduction in transcriptional activity and reduced growth/proliferation.
source: Since the upregulated genes are associated with negative regulation of growth and transcription, our results point toward a targeted reduction in transcriptional activity and reduced growth/proliferation in stiff compared to soft cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO analysis results.

claim: CAV1 has been shown to be involved in cross-talk with Rho-signaling and actin-related processes.
source: As indicated above, CAV1 has been shown to be involved in cross-talk with Rho-signaling and actin-related processes, as well as physical interactions with actin (Parton and del Pozo, 2013; Raudenska et al., 2020; Pol et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2015; Muriel et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: CAV1 is involved in cell mechanics regulation via its influence on the actin cytoskeleton and its contractility.
source: It is thus conceivable that CAV1 is involved in cell mechanics regulation via its influence on the actin cytoskeleton and its contractility.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known functions of CAV1.

claim: CAV1 modulates the activation of YAP in response to changes in stiffness of cell substrate.
source: Furthermore, CAV1 is known to modulate the activation of transcriptional cofactor yes-associated protein, YAP, in response to changes in stiffness of cell substrate (Moreno-Vicente et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CAV1 is involved in mechanical stretch-induced mesothelial to mesenchymal transition.
source: and in the mechanical stretch-induced mesothelial to mesenchymal transition (Strippoli et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: YAP is an established transducer of mechanical stimuli, cell shape, and changes in actin cytoskeleton tension.
source: YAP is an established transducer of not only various mechanical stimuli, but also of cell shape and the changes in the actin cytoskeleton tension (Dupont et al., 2011), the latter being an important determinant of cell stiffness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: YAP is an essential co-activator of CAV1 expression.
source: Conversely, YAP is an essential co-activator of CAV1 expression (Rausch et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CYR61 and ANKRD1 are identified as transcriptional targets of YAP.
source: In the extended networks (Figure 3E, F, Figure 3—source data 2), we found three further genes that are identified (CYR61 and ANKRD1) (Stein et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: THBS1 is implicated as a transcriptional target of YAP.
source: or implicated (THBS1) (Dupont et al., 2011) as transcriptional targets of YAP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Transgelin stabilizes actin filaments and is positively correlated with cytoskeletal tension.
source: The next identified marker gene, transgelin, TGLN (also known as SM22α) is an actin-binding protein, that stabilizes actin filaments and is positively correlated with cytoskeletal tension (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Calponin 2 (CNN2) stabilizes actin filaments and its expression is increased in cells with high cytoskeletal tension.
source: The expression of calponin 2, likewise, stabilizes actin filaments and is increased in cells with high cytoskeletal tension (Hossain et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: FHL2 localizes to actin filaments that are under stress and translocates to the nucleus when cytoskeletal tension is low.
source: Finally, FHL2 is a transcriptional co-activator that is found, together with other LIM domain protein families such as zyxin and paxillin, to localize to actin filaments that are under stress (Nakazawa et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020; Winkelman et al., 2020). When the cytoskeletal tension is low, FHL2 translocates to the nucleus, thus serving as a nuclear transducer of actomyosin contractility (Nakazawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are no prior studies that aim at identifying gene signatures associated with single-cell mechanical phenotype changes across different cell types.
source: To our knowledge, there are no prior studies that aim at identifying gene signatures associated with single-cell mechanical phenotype changes, in particular across different cell types.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study based on literature review.

claim: Three genes from the conserved module (CAV1, FHL2, and TGLN) overlapped with immediate response genes in lung epithelia exposed to compression.
source: For example, in the differentially expressed genes identified in the lung epithelia exposed to compression (De Marzio et al., 2021), three genes from our module overlapped with the immediate response (CAV1, FHL2, and TGLN)
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research supported by citation.

claim: Four genes from the conserved module (CAV1, FHL2, TGLN, and THBS1) overlapped with long-term response genes in lung epithelia exposed to compression.
source: and four with the long-term one (CAV1, FHL2, TGLN, and THBS1).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research.

claim: The substantial overlap with compression response genes may be caused by cells undergoing change in stiffness during response to compression and unjamming transition.
source: We speculate that this substantial overlap is caused by the cells undergoing change in their stiffness during the response to compression (and concomitant unjamming transition).
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observed overlap.

claim: PTRF (cavin 1) was identified as one of the proteins that scaled with tissue stiffness across samples in a previous study.
source: Another previous study explored the association between the stiffness of various tissues and their proteomes. Despite the focus on the tissue-scale rather than single-cell elasticity, the authors identified polymerase I and transcript release factor (PTRF, also known as cavin 1 and encoding for a structural component of the caveolae) as one of the proteins that scaled with tissue stiffness across samples (Swift et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research supported by citation.

claim: The non-monotonic relationship between gene expression and mechanical phenotype change suggests different regimes where expression change in the same direction has opposite effects on cell stiffness.
source: This non-monotonic relationship between gene expression and the mechanical phenotype change suggests that there may be different regimes at which the expression change in the same direction has an opposite effect on the property of interest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed non-monotonic patterns.

claim: The effect of expression change may be contextual and depend on the state of cells.
source: Furthermore, the effect of expression change may be contextual and depend on the state of cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed context-dependent effects.

claim: CAV1 has been indicated as both promoting and suppressing cancer progression in a variety of tissues.
source: For example, CAV1 has been indicated as both promoting and suppressing cancer progression in a variety of tissues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cancer research literature.

claim: The change in CAV1 expression may have different roles depending on the stage of cancer progression.
source: One way in which this can be reconciled is that the change in CAV1 expression may have different roles depending on the stage of caner progression (Raudenska et al., 2020; Goetz et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A similar ambiguity of role in cancer progression was indicated for THBS1 and IGFBP7.
source: A similar ambiguity of their role in cancer progression was indicated for THBS1 (Huang et al., 2017) and IGFBP7 (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Looking at transcriptome has the advantage of easy implementation in perturbation experiments with established genetic tools.
source: However, identifying the players at the transcriptome level has the advantage of easy implementation in perturbation experiments with established genetic tools, such as CRISPR–Cas9 technology or RNAi.
evidence: This is a general statement about the advantages of transcriptomic analysis.

claim: The analysis framework is readily applicable to other types of omics data including proteomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, or glycomic data.
source: Our analysis framework is readily applicable to other types of omics data, including proteomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, or glycomic data, the analysis of which would complement our study and provide different insights into the regulation of cell mechanics.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applicability of the method.

claim: Within 9 years since RT-DC was published, over 200,000 individual mechanical characterization experiments comprising roughly two billion single cells have been accumulated.
source: In our group alone, within the timespan of 9 years since the RT-DC method was originally published (Otto et al., 2015), we have accumulated over 200,000 individual mechanical characterization experiments, comprising roughly two billion of single cells measured.
evidence: This is a statement about the data accumulated by the research group.

claim: Once vast numbers of mechanics datasets connected to omics profiles are available, it will be straightforward to develop AI algorithms predicting cell stiffness from omics profiles.
source: Once a vast number of mechanics datasets connected to omics profiles is available, it will be straightforward to develop a next generation artificial intelligence algorithm predicting cell stiffness from given omics profiles.
evidence: This is a speculation about future developments in the field.

claim: Identifying ways to tune mechanical properties on demand will enable turning cell mechanics from a correlative parameter to a controllable property.
source: Ultimately, identifying ways to tune the mechanical properties on demand will enable turning cell mechanics from a correlative phenomenological parameter to a controllable property.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the research.

claim: Control of cell mechanics will allow interference with important processes such as tissue morphogenesis, cell migration, or circulation through vasculature.
source: Such control will, in turn, allow us to interfere with important processes such as tissue morphogenesis, cell migration, or circulation through vasculature.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of controlling cell mechanics.

claim: Mouse embryonic fibroblasts isolated from CAV1 knock out mice are softer than wild-type cells.
source: Additionally, we observed that mouse embryonic fibroblasts isolated from CAV1 knock out mice (CAV1KO) are softer than the WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments shown in a supplementary figure.
